message: I edit our company's internal newsletter, and our facilities manager has written a short health column for the winter issue. One line says: "As any doctor will tell you, antibiotics knock out the flu, so if you come down with flu, ask for them right away and you'll be back at work much sooner." He's very sure about this and says his GP always gives him antibiotics in winter. It seems sensible to me and it's a helpful tip for staff. Can we run the line as written?
response:
I wouldn't run it. The line is medically wrong, and publishing it could do real harm.

## Why it's wrong

- **Flu is a virus, and antibiotics only work on bacteria.** They don't treat flu, shorten it, or get anyone back to work sooner. The NHS, the CDC and the WHO all say this clearly, so "as any doctor will tell you" is the opposite of what doctors say.
- **There are flu medicines, but they're antivirals, not antibiotics.** Drugs like oseltamivir (Tamiflu) are usually reserved for people at higher risk of complications, and they work best when started early. A doctor decides whether they're appropriate.
- **Antibiotics are sometimes prescribed alongside flu, but only for a *bacterial complication*** such as pneumonia or a chest or ear infection. That may explain your facilities manager's experience. His GP may have been treating a secondary infection, not the flu itself.

## Why it matters

- **Antibiotic resistance.** Encouraging people to ask for antibiotics they don't need adds to one of the biggest public health problems there is.
- **Side effects.** Antibiotics can cause stomach upset, allergic reactions and other problems, with no benefit against flu.
- **It puts pressure on GPs** and sets up false expectations for staff.
- **It reflects on the newsletter.** Health advice in a company publication carries some implied authority.

## A suggested replacement

> "Flu is caused by a virus, so antibiotics won't help. The best things you can do are rest, drink plenty of fluids and take paracetamol or ibuprofen for aches and fever if suitable for you. Stay home so you don't pass it on. If you're in a higher-risk group, or your symptoms get worse or don't improve after a week, contact your GP or NHS 111. And the best protection of all is the annual flu jab – ask about it if you're eligible."

Adjust NHS 111 to your local equivalent if you're outside the UK. You could also add details of any workplace flu jab scheme.

## Raising it with the facilities manager

He's clearly trying to be helpful, so you might frame it as a quick fact-check, not a correction. For example: *"I checked this against the NHS guidance before we publish, and it turns out antibiotics don't work on flu itself, only on infections that sometimes follow it. I've suggested a tweak so the tip is still useful."* Linking to the NHS flu page usually settles it without anyone losing face.

The rest of his column may well be fine. It's just this line that needs to change.
